title: Class 6 Maths Knowing Our Numbers: Chapter 1 Study Guide + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 6 Maths Knowing Our Numbers Guide
meta_desc: Class 6 Maths Knowing Our Numbers made clear: large numbers, Indian vs international commas, estimation and Roman numerals, with solved case studies.
excerpt: NCERT Class 6 Chapter 1 looks simple until a 7-digit number turns up with commas in the wrong places. Here is a clear walkthrough of Knowing Our Numbers, plus two solved case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write the number seventy-six lakh on the board and ask a fresh Class 6 group to put in the commas, and you will get four different answers. That single moment is why class 6 maths knowing our numbers is the chapter I never rush. NCERT puts it first for a reason: everything from money sums to data handling later in the year rests on reading big numbers correctly and knowing roughly how large they are. Get commas and estimation wrong here and the mistakes follow a student for years.

This chapter is not hard, but it is fiddly. There are four skills hiding inside it, and most children are shaky on two of them. Let me take you through each, then walk through two case studies of the kind the NCERT exercises actually ask.

Reading and writing large numbers

Class 6 pushes numbers past the six-digit line a child met in Class 5. Now you are handling lakhs, ten-lakhs and crores. The core idea stays the same — each digit sits in a place worth ten times the one on its right — but the sheer length trips people up. My advice: always read a number in groups, never digit by digit. The number 5074320 is not ‘five zero seven…’; it is ‘fifty lakh, seventy-four thousand, three hundred twenty.’

Place value is the anchor

Ask what the 7 is worth in 5074320 and a weak student says ‘seven’. It is worth 70,000. Drilling place value out loud — ‘which place, how much is it worth’ — fixes more errors than any worksheet.

Indian vs international system — the comma trap

This is where class 6 maths knowing our numbers earns its reputation. The two systems group digits differently, so the commas land in different spots.

  • Indian system: commas after 3 digits, then every 2 — thousand, lakh, crore.
  • International system: commas every 3 digits — thousand, million, billion.
DigitsIndian systemInternational system
765432176,54,3217,654,321
520340052,03,4005,203,400
900000009,00,00,000 (9 crore)90,000,000 (90 million)

My one rule for students: decide which system the question wants before you touch the pen. Half the errors I mark are correct numbers with commas from the wrong system.

Comparing and ordering numbers

Comparing is quick once children stop counting on fingers and count digits instead. More digits means a bigger number, full stop. Only when the digit-count ties do you compare left to right, place by place. Ordering a list into ascending or descending order is just this comparison repeated — and this is exactly what forming the greatest and smallest number from given digits tests.

Estimation and rounding

Here is the counter-intuitive bit students resist: sometimes the wrong-looking answer is the right one. Estimation asks for a sensible round figure, not the exact total. To estimate 6789 + 3212, round each to the nearest thousand (7000 + 3000) and answer 10,000. Round to nearest ten, hundred or thousand depending on what the question says — and always check your exact answer against the estimate. If they are wildly apart, you slipped somewhere.

Roman numerals

The chapter closes with Roman numerals, which children usually enjoy because they feel like a code. The seven symbols are I (1), V (5), X (10), L (50), C (100), D (500), M (1000). Two rules do most of the work: if a smaller symbol comes before a larger one you subtract (IV = 4, IX = 9, XL = 40), otherwise you add (VI = 6, XV = 15). There is no symbol for zero, and you never repeat V, L or D.

Case study 1: the district census

Read the passage the way the exam presents it. A district office records the population of three towns as: Town A 3,45,600; Town B 2,98,750; Town C 3,45,060.

  • Which town has the largest population? All three are six digits, so compare place by place. Town A and Town C both start 3,45; at the hundreds place A has 6 and C has 0, so Town A (3,45,600) is largest.
  • Write Town B in the international system. 2,98,750 regrouped every three digits is 298,750.
  • Estimate the total population to the nearest thousand. Round to 3,46,000 + 2,99,000 + 3,45,000 = 9,90,000. About nine lakh ninety thousand people.

Notice how one passage tested comparing, the two systems, and estimation together. That blend is exactly how NCERT case studies are built.

Case study 2: the school clock and library

A school library shelf is labelled with Roman numerals, and a donation drive collects money. Shelf numbers run I to XX; the drive collects ₹47,890 in week one and ₹39,240 in week two.

  • What is shelf XIV in ordinary numbers? XIV = 10 + 4 = 14.
  • Write ₹47,890 in words (Indian system). Forty-seven thousand eight hundred ninety.
  • Estimate the two-week total to the nearest thousand. 48,000 + 39,000 = 87,000, so roughly ₹87,000 was collected.

Solving these two passages start to finish is worth more than twenty isolated sums, because it forces a student to pick the right skill for each part — the real test of whether the chapter has landed.

Try the quiz, then the case studies

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering every idea above — place value, both comma systems, comparing, estimation and Roman numerals. Attempt it, then read the explanations for anything you miss. When you want longer, exam-style practice, the printable case-study e-book at the end gives full passages with step-by-step solutions.

quiz.title: Class 6 Knowing Our Numbers Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on large numbers, Indian and international commas, comparing, estimation and Roman numerals. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 6 Maths Chapter 1: Knowing Our Numbers

questions.q: How is 7654321 written with commas in the Indian place-value system?
questions.explanation: The Indian system puts a comma after the first 3 digits, then after every 2 digits: 76,54,321.

questions.q: In the international system, 5203400 is written as:
questions.explanation: The international system groups every 3 digits from the right: 5,203,400.

questions.q: Which of these is the greatest number?
questions.explanation: All are five digits, so compare from the left. 55,001 has the largest ten-thousands and thousands digits.

questions.q: What is the smallest five-digit number?
questions.explanation: 9,999 has only four digits. The smallest five-digit number is 10,000.

questions.q: Estimate 6789 + 3212 by rounding each number to the nearest thousand.
questions.explanation: 6789 rounds to 7000 and 3212 rounds to 3000, giving 7000 + 3000 = 10,000.
A smaller symbol before a larger one means subtract: XL = 50 − 10 = 40. You never write four X’s in a row.

questions.q: What number does the Roman numeral XIV stand for?
What is the place value of the digit 7 in 3,74,281?
questions.explanation: The 7 sits in the ten-thousands place, so its value is 70,000.

faq.q: What topics are in Class 6 Maths Chapter 1, Knowing Our Numbers?
faq.a: The chapter covers reading and writing large numbers, place value, the Indian and international systems of commas, comparing and ordering numbers, estimation and rounding, and Roman numerals.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Indian and international number systems?
faq.a: The Indian system places commas after 3 digits and then every 2 digits (thousand, lakh, crore). The international system places a comma after every 3 digits (thousand, million, billion). So 7654321 is 76,54,321 in the Indian system and 7,654,321 in the international system.

faq.q: How do I estimate a sum in this chapter?
faq.a: Round each number to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand as the question asks, then add the rounded values. For example, 6789 + 3212 rounds to 7000 + 3000 = 10,000. Always compare your estimate with the exact answer to catch mistakes.

faq.q: What are the basic rules for Roman numerals?
faq.a: The symbols are I, V, X, L, C, D and M. If a smaller symbol comes before a larger one you subtract (IV = 4, XL = 40); otherwise you add (VI = 6, XV = 15). There is no symbol for zero, and V, L and D are never repeated.
